question: A recent study1 carried out for Parliament’s TRAN Committee found that public charging is still significantly more expensive than charging at home or at work and often appears unreasonably high, non-transparent, complex and not user-friendly2, undermining the transition to e-mobility and the cost reasoning behind buying a car, especially for citizens for whom home charging is not an option.

In addition, the same charging session often leads to different final costs depending on the provider, app, card or payment method used by the consumer and price information is often not available for consumers before charging starts3.

Although Article 5 of the AFIR stipulates that public charging prices must be reasonable, easily and clearly comparable, transparent and non-discriminatory, its implementation and enforcement remain incomplete, fragmented and uneven. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What measures does it intend to take to address excessively high, non-transparent and insufficiently justified charging prices for electric vehicles in the EU?

Does it intend to revise the AFIR and propose minimum EU requirements to improve price transparency, such as the mandatory display of the total charging price before charging begins, including all surcharges, as well as the mandatory display, before charging, of both the MSP price and the ad hoc charging price?

See https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2026/759345/CASP_STU(2026)759345_EN.pdf. 2 Average AC charging prices through mobility service providers range from EUR 0.27/kWh to EUR 0.65/kWh, while for DC charging the range is even wider, from EUR 0.32 to EUR 0.85, with the highest prices exceeding EUR 1.00/kWh in some markets.
Even at the same charging station, the difference between the highest and lowest price usually ranges from EUR 0.40 to EUR 1.00 and in extreme cases can reach EUR 1.40/kWh.

3 According to the study, price information is often not displayed before charging starts, the price calculation method is difficult for consumers to understand and the final price depends to a large degree on whether the user pays ad hoc via a charge point operator (CPO) or a mobility service provider (MSP/roaming), sometimes including hidden charges. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure1 (AFIR) sets clear rules on how operators of recharging points and mobility service providers must make price information available to consumers.

Article 5 of the Regulation requires that prices charged by operators of publicly accessible recharging points and by mobility service providers must be reasonable, easily and clearly comparable, transparent and non-discriminatory. The regulation equally requires that those operators must make available all relevant price information prior to the start of the recharging session.

Article 5(6) also requires Member States to monitor the recharging market in particular with regards to those price transparency provisions. The Commission is currently reviewing Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 in accordance with Article 24 of the Regulation. This review addresses, among others, user aspects, including on price transparency and enforcement aspects.

The study commissioned by the Parliament’s Committee on Transport and Tourism (TRAN Committee) will serve as one input to the ongoing impact assessment. As announced in the Commission Communication COM (2025) 95 final2 the Commission plans to adopt a proposal for the revision of AFIR by the end of this year.
1 Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 September 2023 on the

deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure, and repealing Directive 2014/94/EU, OJ L 234, 22.9.2023, pp. 1– 47. 2 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions Industrial Action Plan for the European automotive sector, COM/2025/95 final.
